overview.summary: Game developers design and build video games, combining programming, art, sound and story.
overview.problems: They create experiences people enjoy, from mobile puzzles to large console worlds, and make sure they run smoothly.
overview.worksWith: Designers, artists, writers, sound designers, testers, producers and other programmers.
overview.workplaces: Game studios, large publishers, small independent teams, and freelance or solo work, often in offices or remotely.

timeline.title: Team stand-up
timeline.description: The team shares progress and plans the day.
timeline.why: Games involve many specialists whose work must fit together.

timeline.title: Programming features
timeline.description: The developer writes code for character movement, game rules or menus and tests it in the game.
timeline.why: Smooth play depends on well-built systems.

timeline.title: Fixing bugs
timeline.description: The developer finds why something behaves wrongly, such as a character stuck in a wall, and fixes it.
timeline.why: Bugs break the feeling of play.

timeline.title: Playtesting and feedback
timeline.description: The developer plays the latest version, watches other people play and notes what is confusing or boring.
timeline.why: Fun has to be tested, not assumed.

timeline.title: Working with artists and designers
timeline.description: The developer adjusts code to fit new art, sound or level designs.
timeline.why: A game feels right when all its parts work together.

timeline.title: Crunch before deadlines
timeline.description: Some studios work longer hours before a release.

responsibilities: Building game features such as controls, physics and artificial intelligence
Working with designers, artists and testers
Making games run on different devices
challenges: Crunch time before releases can mean long hours in some studios.
The industry is competitive and jobs can be unstable, with studios closing or projects cancelled.
Projects can be cancelled after a lot of work.
Pay can be lower than in other software jobs in some places.
Finishing a game takes many different skills and a lot of persistence.
workEnvironment: Mostly desk and computer based, in studios or remotely, working in teams with regular meetings and play sessions. Hours are often regular but can lengthen before a release. Independent developers work alone or in very small teams.
rewards: Creating something people play and enjoy
A mix of art, logic and story
tradeoffs: Pay and conditions that vary by country and studio

activity.title: Design a simple game and test it
steps: Invent a simple game for two players using paper, dice or cards, with a clear goal and three rules.
Play it with a friend and watch for moments that are confusing or boring.
Change one rule and play again.
If you want to try coding, make a very small version with a free beginner tool such as Scratch.
Note which part you enjoyed most: designing, testing or building.
activity.outcome: You practise designing rules, testing with players and improving, which is the core loop of game development.
activity.safety: Use your own ideas and images, do not share personal details online, and ask an adult before creating accounts on any website.

source: Written by Futurixia from general knowledge of how this profession works. It is illustrative and is not based on interviews or surveys.
